lead: Brow henna, also called henna brows, is a semi-permanent way of tinting eyebrow hair and the skin beneath it with a paste made from powdered henna leaves. It is offered mainly in brow salons and is also sold as an at-home kit, and people use it to make sparse, pale or patchy brows look darker, fuller and more defined.[1]

Henna's dye, lawsone, is released when the leaves are dried, powdered and mixed into a paste, and it binds to proteins in the outer layer of skin.[1] On skin the stain starts orange and darkens to reddish brown over about three days, then fades through exfoliation over one to three weeks.[1] On hair, results run from orange to burgundy depending on the starting colour, and cassia or indigo can shift the shade lighter or darker.[1] Wikipedia notes henna has also been used as a temporary substitute for eyebrow pencil.[1]

Eyebrows are central to facial expression; research cited on Wikipedia suggests communication is their main role, and brow shape has changed through fashion history.[2] The main documented safety concern is with products sold as black henna, which often contain para-phenylenediamine (PPD) and have been linked to severe allergic reactions.[1]

angle.text: Henna stains the brow hairs and the skin between them, so brows look fuller and the shape reads more clearly. The colour fades over days to weeks without daily makeup.

paras: The leaves hold lawsone, which stays locked in until they are dried, powdered and mixed with a liquid such as water, lemon juice or tea. The paste releases most of its dye within about two to six days, so it is used fresh.[1] Lawsone binds to proteins in the skin's outer layer, which is why the skin under the brow stains along with the hair.[1]

Henna on hair gives results from orange to auburn to burgundy depending on the starting hair colour, and practitioners sometimes blend it with plant dyes such as cassia or indigo to alter the shade.[1] Henna has also been used as a temporary eyebrow-pencil substitute and for eyebrow embroidery.[1]

The eyebrow keeps sweat and debris out of the eye and conveys emotion, and mobile brows help express subtle feelings such as recognition and sympathy.[2] Cosmetic options listed include tinting, microblading, threading, tweezing, waxing, brow gels, pencils and powders, transplants and brow lifts.[2] Fashions have varied: Japanese people in the 8th century shaved or plucked brows and painted new ones higher on the forehead, Elizabethan high-status women sometimes removed brows entirely, thin plucked brows returned in the 1920s and 1930s, and shaved brow lines were popular in the 1990s and 2000s.[2]

Ancient Egyptians used henna on hair, skin and nails, and its use later spread through the Maghreb, the Indian subcontinent and parts of Eastern Europe.[1] Its use as a brow tint is comparatively recent.[1]

Natural henna rarely causes harm beyond occasional mild allergies, usually linked to lemon juice or essential oils rather than henna itself, but commercial pastes may contain undisclosed additives, including PPD.[1] Henna can be dangerous for people with G6PD deficiency.[1]

Products marketed as black henna often are not henna and can contain PPD at concentrations of 10 to 80 percent, compared with a limit below 6 percent for hair dyes. Reactions typically appear 3 to 12 days after application, can include blistering and permanent scarring, and sensitisation can be lifelong, affecting later exposure to hair dyes.[1] Warning signs listed include a paste that stains skin black within half an hour.[1]

In the United States the FDA allows henna only as a hair dye under a grandfather clause and has not approved it for direct application to skin; PPD is prohibited as a skin stain.[1] Because brow henna is applied close to the eye, labelling and regulatory status differ between countries.

name: Brow henna

card.summary: A plant-based semi-permanent stain for brows that lasts days to weeks; the main documented risk is adulterated 'black henna' products containing PPD.
card.note: Black henna products may contain PPD, linked to severe allergic reactions; FDA has not approved henna for skin.

quick.overview:
Brow henna is a paste made from powdered henna leaves that stains brow hairs and the skin underneath, making brows look darker and more filled in. It is done in salons or with at-home kits.

The colour is temporary, with the skin stain generally fading over one to three weeks. No clinical studies specific to eyebrow henna were found.
quick.mechanism: The lawsone dye in henna binds to the keratin in hair and the outer skin layer, producing an orange-to-reddish-brown stain that darkens over a few days.
quick.risks: Natural henna is regarded differently from products sold as black henna, which often contain PPD and have been linked to severe allergic reactions and scarring. The US FDA has not approved henna for direct skin application.
